blocks.md: Every app you will ever build talks to the outside world. Real data does not live in `useState` — it comes across a network, arrives asynchronously, and arrives in a shape you have to describe in TypeScript before you can safely use it. This session is the bridge between 'I know the syntax' and 'I can ship a real feature'. You will fetch live recipes from a public API, type every corner of the response, and handle every state the UI can land in — loading, empty, error, and results. When this is done, you will have a pattern you can drop into any future project.

blocks.canDo: build a typed app that fetches live data
blocks.md: **By the end of this session you will be able to:** build a React + TypeScript app that takes a search query, fetches results from a real public API, types the response with an interface, and renders a grid of cards — with distinct loading, empty, and error states. Zero `any` in your own code.

**Your build plan — keep this open as you code:**

1. **Scaffold** — `npm create vite@latest recipe-search -- --template react-ts`, then `npm install && npm run dev`.
2. **Type the API shape** — write a `Meal` interface that matches the fields you will use from the TheMealDB response (`idMeal`, `strMeal`, `strMealThumb`, `strCategory`). The API search endpoint is `https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/search.php?s=chicken`.
3. **State first** — three pieces of state in `App`: `query` (string), `meals` (Meal[]), and `status` ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'done').
4. **Fetch** — a `handleSearch` async function that sets status to 'loading', awaits `fetch`, types the JSON, sets `meals`, sets status to 'done'. Wrap in try/catch for the error state.
5. **Search form** — a controlled `<input>` plus a Search button; on submit call `handleSearch`.
6. **Results grid** — map over `meals` and render a `<MealCard>` component. Show the right UI for each status value.

**API reference — free, public test key embedded in the URL, no sign-up needed**

TheMealDB is a free recipe API that uses the public test key `1` in the URL path — you can see it in `v1/1/search.php`. The search endpoint returns a JSON object with a `meals` array (or `null` when nothing matches).
blocks.label: TheMealDB API docs — free, public test key in URL

blocks.md: **Tip — type the response, not just the data.** The full JSON shape from TheMealDB is `{ meals: Meal[] | null }`. Model that wrapper type too: `type MealSearchResponse = { meals: Meal[] | null }`. Then you can cast with `const data = await res.json() as MealSearchResponse` and TypeScript knows `data.meals` can be null — which forces you to handle the empty state cleanly.

blocks.task:
Create a new Vite + React + TypeScript project and build a **recipe search app** using TheMealDB (`https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/search.php?s=QUERY` — free, public test key `1` is already embedded in the URL, no sign-up needed).

Your app must:

- Define a `Meal` interface covering at least `idMeal`, `strMeal`, `strMealThumb`, and `strCategory`.
- Have a **search form** (controlled input + button) that triggers a fetch when submitted.
- Show a **loading indicator** while the request is in flight.
- Render a **grid of `<MealCard>` components** when results arrive — each card shows the meal image, name, and category.
- Show a friendly **empty message** when the API returns no matches.
- Show a friendly **error message** when the fetch fails.
- Contain **zero `any`** in your own source files — TypeScript strict mode must stay on.

Getting stuck is completely normal and expected — try it yourself first, and if you need a full guided walkthrough, one is just one click away.
blocks.definitionOfDone: Type a search term (try 'chicken'), see a loading state, then see real recipe cards from the API with image, name, and category. Search for gibberish — see the empty message. The TypeScript compiler reports zero errors and you have no `any` in your own files.
hints: **Set up the fetch and types first.** Create a `Meal` interface and a `MealSearchResponse` type (`{ meals: Meal[] | null }`). Write an async `fetchMeals(query: string): Promise<Meal[]>` function that calls `fetch('https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/search.php?s=' + encodeURIComponent(query))`, casts the JSON with `as MealSearchResponse`, and returns `data.meals ?? []`. Verify it logs results before touching any React state.

**Wire up the search input and state.** In `App.tsx` add three state variables: `const [query, setQuery] = useState('')`, `const [meals, setMeals] = useState<Meal[]>([])`, and `const [status, setStatus] = useState<'idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'done'>('idle')`. Write `handleSearch` as an async function: set status to `'loading'`, call `fetchMeals(query)`, set `meals` with the result and status to `'done'`, catch errors and set status to `'error'`. Hook it to a `<form onSubmit>` so pressing Enter or the button fires it.

**Render the results grid and all UI states.** Create a `MealCard` component that accepts a `meal: Meal` prop and renders the image (`strMealThumb`), name (`strMeal`), and category (`strCategory`) in a card. Back in `App.tsx`, conditionally render: a spinner/text when `status === 'loading'`; the card grid with `meals.map(m => <MealCard key={m.idMeal} meal={m} />)` when `status === 'done' && meals.length > 0`; an empty message when `status === 'done' && meals.length === 0`; an error message when `status === 'error'`.

blocks.md:
You just shipped a typed, API-driven React app from a blank project — a search form, live network requests, a typed response shape, a results grid, and every UI state a real user will hit. You wrote zero `any`, which means TypeScript was working *for* you the whole time.

That is Phase 4 complete. You know TypeScript, you know how to type React state and props, and you can fetch and display real data safely. The next step is a short quiz to seal it all in.
bullets: Type the full API response shape — including null and wrapper objects — before you touch the data
Model async UI with a status enum ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'done') — four states, four branches
Zero `any` is achievable: cast once at the network boundary, then let types flow through
A reusable fetch helper keeps your component logic clean and easy to test
